Since this occurs after Michael's request to post this elsewhere and I still see it here, and sionce John seems to be asking specifically about the binomial expansion I assume I'm allowed to respond both mathematically and here. Michael?

Anyway, assuming I am allowed to answer a specific mathematical query without being penalised for using mathematiucs, and assuming I can answer here where the question was posed.

 The reason for the "2" "not" being used is that due to the vector nature of electronmagnetic radiation, the expansion is done in complex numbers. The Intensity profile of a beam is given as the cmplex square of the complex amplitude modulation. Thus, if the two plane beams are given as:

A_1 = A_01*exp(i((k1_x*sin(theta) + k1_y*cos(theta)) - wt))

and

A_2 = A_02*exp(i((k2_x*sin(theta) + k2_y*cos(theta)) - wt))

Then, clearly from De Moivres Theorem, this forms the solution set of a second order partial differential equation. Without too much detail (which can be provided if more detail is required or further questions are posed), the full set of the four partial differential equations from Faraday's experimental observatiuons can be reduced to a second order partial differential equation in two variables. However, if we now add in the Lorentz foce equation and Poynting's Theorem, the power is seen as the amplitude multiplied by it's own complex conjugate. The complex conjugate brings in the phase relationships that are coded into the complex amplitude that make interference possible. The same for the triple binomial expansion.

Actually, you're completely right! It's also bloody frustrating! Maybe this frustration/anger shows through sometimes You may remember that essay I wrote a while back comparing the rise of the engineer against the rise of the scientist.

Engineers take the knowledge they need to carry out their function. There's some mathematical knowledge necessary but mostly nothing fundemental.You don't need to know the theory of differential equations to build a bridge or make a hologram. However, the education of the engineer involves some fundemental physics and mathematics and so a lot of engineers think they "know" physics and mathematics. Conversely, when a physicist/mathematician can't build a bridge, the engineers then say/boast/crow that they can do this "better than any scientist". This partial knowledge then leads engineers to "dabble" in physics without understanding the depth of the problem and gain kudos because of their partial ability in mathematics and physics. A case in point: When I was an electronics engineer, I subscribed to a magazine called "Wireless World" - a magazine for electronic engineers. Over a particular period - about 5 or so issues - the magazine and it's readers debated the Twin paradox in relativity. They refused to believe there was no paradox and they would not let it go! They were firmly convinced that engineers could solve problems in theoretical physics! Ihave an engineer friend who's an excellant engineer and inventor, many patents to his name, who's convinced that the ether exists and that cold fusion is real. However, when I point out that relativity doesn't exactly say "There is no ether", it just says, "It doesn't matter whether there is or not" he gets confused. He doesn't grasp the irrelevance of any specific inertial frame as opposed to it's existence

So, to an "engineer", does it matter how light behaves? Not at all! Whether it's photons or little green men with pink spots, if you get your ratio right and your exposure right and your development right, you'll get a good hologram. If you don't, it's a matter of tweaking these parameters, not solving partial differential equations. Who cares about those?! If you're inventing a gadget to do anything from milking a cow to flying to the moon, all you need is the extent of knowledge necessary to "do" your function. Any deep thoughts on Quantum Field Theory should be as foreign to an engineer as the colour codes on resistors should be to a theoretical physicist. Another case in point. When I finally left physics, I became an electronic engineer working on Britain's first digital telephone exchange system (System X to those who know what that is). As I left Salaam for the last time, he asked, "What's a digital telephone exchange" Here was a Nobel Laureate asking what I thought was obvious! 

By the way, Joy is an engineer. She build's 'em and makes 'em work. If any theory is required, I provide it. I sometimes complain that her designs won't work for this reason or that. I'm usually wrong. Meanwhile, I "invented", "created" whatever, a holographic amplifier system using the theory of resonance to resonate two sets of Bragg planes. Apparently 2 units of light went into the hologram and 2.3 units of light came out. She refused to accept this because she didn't understand resonance. Finally, the two of us and Prof Denisyuk were having a coffee when she said, "Ask him". I explained the system to Denisyuk and he said that, of course, it would look like an amplification because more light would come out then go in. Now she believed me!
